stops.name: La Albuera, the bloodiest field of the Peninsula
stops.campa: Under Beresford, in the allied line at La Albuera, San Martín fights his last great battle in the service of Spain. The field is a slaughterhouse: whole brigades fall where they stand under the rain, and the veteran of Oran, Roussillon and Bailén reads in the carnage the exhaustion of the old world. His resolve is already turned westward: within weeks he will ask leave to quit Spain, carrying to America everything her wars have taught him.

stops.name: Cádiz, barrio de San Carlos: the oath of the Rational Knights
stops.campa: In an apartment of the San Carlos quarter, where young Carlos de Alvear keeps lodge, the Society of Caballeros Racionales No. 3 receives Lieutenant Colonel San Martín. Candles, drawn swords, the American brothers around him, he swears the oath: to work for the independence of America, and never to recognize as legitimate any government of his homeland but one elected by the free and spontaneous will of the peoples. From this night the King's officer is the Revolution's man; the rest of his life is the keeping of this word.
stops.quote: No reconocerás por gobierno legítimo de tu patria sino a aquel que sea elegido por la libre y espontánea voluntad de los pueblos, y trabajarás por la independencia absoluta de América.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Caballeros Racionales / Lautaro lodges, preserved in the lodge papers and in San Martín's own hand (per the Gran Logia de la Argentina and Mitre)

stops.name: Bahía de Cádiz, the sea-gate opens
stops.campa: His discharge obtained on the pretext of ill health and business in Lima, San Martín boards an English vessel and stands out of the bay of Cádiz. Twenty-two years of Spanish service fall astern with the white city. He carries a passport, a small purse, and the oath. The brothers of the lodge have marked the route: London first, the house of Miranda, and then the river of his childhood. He never sets foot in Spain again.

stops.name: London, Grafton Street: the house of Miranda
stops.campa: Four months in London. San Martín goes to the house in Grafton Street where Francisco de Miranda, Precursor of American liberty, kept his archive and his lodge; there the Gran Reunión Americana receives him, and with Zapiola he is raised to the fifth degree. Around the table: Alvear, Andrés Bello, López Méndez, the scattered priesthood of a continent not yet born. In a London shop he buys a curved Damascus sabre, the corvo that will ride with him from San Lorenzo to the last codicil of his will.

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic aboard the George Canning
stops.campa: Fifty days of ocean aboard the English frigate George Canning, out of London on 19 January. On her deck the lodge travels entire: San Martín, Alvear, Zapiola, Chilavert, Holmberg, officers formed in Europe's wars, returning like seeds on the wind. They drill their plans as the ship crosses the line; the veteran of Bailén, thirty-four years old, watches the Southern Cross climb the night. Every mile of this wake is the oath being kept.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the landing of 9 March 1812
stops.campa: The George Canning anchors in the roads of Buenos Aires and the Gazeta notes among the arrivals a lieutenant colonel of cavalry, José de San Martín. He is a stranger in his own patria: American-born, Spanish-formed, watched with suspicion by the drawing rooms. The Triumvirate recognizes his rank within days. The child who left at five returns at thirty-four, bearing a sabre from London and a mandate from a lodge; and the Revolution, without yet knowing it, has received its general.

stops.name: Retiro, forging the Granaderos a Caballo
stops.campa: One week ashore, San Martín receives authority to raise a squadron of mounted grenadiers. On the Retiro field he builds a corps as one builds a creed: European drill, the sabre stroke taught by his own hand, a secret tribunal of honor where officers judge officers: cowardice, a lie, an insult to a woman, all punished by expulsion. Sons of the provinces are made into the first professional soldiers of the Revolution. From this square of dust will ride the escort of three liberated nations.

stops.name: Buenos Aires Cathedral, marriage to Remedios de Escalada
stops.campa: In the cathedral of Buenos Aires, Father Luis Chorroarín blesses the marriage of the thirty-four-year-old colonel and María de los Remedios de Escalada, fifteen, daughter of one of the city's great patriot houses; Carlos de Alvear and his wife stand witness. The drawing rooms murmur at the difference in years; the canon answers that Remedios will earn her epitaph: wife and friend, donating her jewels for his army, embroidering his flag, dying while he liberates a continent.

stops.name: Plaza de la Victoria, the revolution of 8 October 1812
stops.campa: The First Triumvirate falters, suppresses news of the victory of Tucumán, clings to power. At dawn the Granaderos a Caballo stand formed in the Plaza de la Victoria, San Martín and Alvear at their head, the Lautaro lodge moving behind the scene like a hand behind a curtain. Without a shot, the government falls; a Second Triumvirate is sworn, pledged to summon an assembly and speak the word independence. The lodge has shown its method: force, exactly measured, in the service of the oath.

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the convent field
stops.campa: From the tower of the convent of San Carlos, San Martín watches the Spanish ships on the Paraná. At dawn his hundred and twenty grenadiers burst from behind the monastery walls in two wings. Grapeshot kills his horse; pinned beneath it, a royalist bayonet descending, he is saved by Baigorria's lance and by the grenadier Juan Bautista Cabral, who takes the blow and dies of it, saying: 'Muero contento, hemos batido al enemigo.' Fifteen minutes of combat; the river gate of the Revolution is closed forever. Under the pine of the convent the commander writes his dispatch.

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto, the meeting with Belgrano
stops.campa: At the post-house of Yatasto on the Salta road, the tradition sets the meeting of the two swords of the Revolution: Belgrano, riding south with the wreck of the Army of the North after Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, and San Martín, riding north to relieve him. The defeated general offers his command with humility; the new one receives it with reverence, and asks the veteran to stay and teach him the country. Two founders embrace at a crossroads of defeat, and the canon keeps the place holy.
stops.quote: Es lo mejor que tenemos en la América del Sur.
stops.quote_source: San Martín on Belgrano, letter to Tomás Godoy Cruz, 1816

stops.name: Tucumán, La Ciudadela: command of the Army of the North
stops.campa: In the fortified camp of La Ciudadela outside Tucumán, San Martín takes command of the broken Army of the North and rebuilds it: drill, sanitation, a school of officers, the methods of Retiro applied at scale. Studying the maps he reaches the heresy that becomes the strategy of the continent: Upper Peru is a corridor of defeats; the road to Lima does not go up through the altiplano. He gives the mountain frontier to Güemes and his gauchos to hold, and begins, in silence, to think of Chile.
